net-ipv4-int.title: IPv4 Address and Integer Conversion
net-ipv4-int.description:
An IPv4 address is just a 32-bit unsigned number. The dotted form `a.b.c.d` writes its four bytes in
decimal, most significant byte first (network byte order).

Write `ipv4_convert(value)` that converts in **both directions**:

- if `value` is a string such as `"192.168.1.10"`, return the integer `a*2^24 + b*2^16 + c*2^8 + d`;
- if `value` is an integer in `[0, 2^32 - 1]`, return the dotted string with no leading zeros.

All inputs are valid.

**Example:** `"10.0.0.1"` → `167772161`

**Example:** `3232235786` → `"192.168.1.10"`

guide.prereqs: Bit shifts and masks; the lesson *IPv4 addressing, subnets, CIDR and NAT*.
guide.intuition: Treat the address as a base-256 number with four digits. Reading it is the same loop you would use to parse a decimal string, with 256 in place of 10; writing it peels the digits off with shifts and a `& 255` mask.
hints: Which of the four numbers is worth the most? The leftmost one is multiplied by 2^24.
Accumulate with `n = n * 256 + part` (or `(n << 8) | part`) while walking the parts left to right.
For the reverse direction, `(value >> 24) & 255` is the first octet, `(value >> 16) & 255` the second, and so on.
guide.brute_force: Multiply each octet by an explicit power of 256 and add; for the reverse use repeated `divmod(value, 256)` and reverse the digits. Both are O(1), so there is nothing slower to improve on; the bit version is simply the idiomatic one.
guide.approach:
1. If the input is a string, split on `.` and fold: start with `n = 0`, then for each part `n = (n << 8) | int(part)`.
2. Otherwise extract the bytes with shifts of 24, 16, 8 and 0, masking each with 255, and join with dots.

**Dry run** for `"10.0.0.1"`: `n=10` → `10*256+0 = 2560` → `2560*256+0 = 655360` → `655360*256+1 = 167772161`.
Reverse: `167772161 >> 24 = 10`, `(>>16)&255 = 0`, `(>>8)&255 = 0`, `&255 = 1` → `10.0.0.1`.
guide.complexity: Time O(1) and space O(1): always four octets.
guide.pitfalls: Reversing the byte order (little-endian) gives a valid-looking but wrong number. Concatenating the decimal digits is not the same as base 256. Remember `0` must print as `0.0.0.0`, not an empty string.
guide.follow_up: Add validation (exactly four parts, each 0–255, no leading zeros), or support IPv6 with eight 16-bit groups and `::` compression.

net-cidr-contains.title: Is an Address Inside a CIDR Block?
net-cidr-contains.description:
A CIDR block `a.b.c.d/p` names every address whose first `p` bits equal the first `p` bits of `a.b.c.d`.

Write `in_cidr(ip, cidr)` returning `True` when the dotted IPv4 address `ip` belongs to the block.

- `p` is between 0 and 32. `/0` contains every address; `/32` contains exactly one.
- The block may be written with host bits set (`"10.9.8.7/8"` means the same as `"10.0.0.0/8"`).

**Example:** `ip = "192.168.5.130"`, `cidr = "192.168.5.128/25"` → `True`

**Example:** `ip = "192.168.5.127"`, `cidr = "192.168.5.128/25"` → `False`
net-cidr-contains.starter:
def in_cidr(ip: str, cidr: str) -> bool:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Problem *IPv4 Address and Integer Conversion*; bitwise AND.
guide.intuition: Membership is a comparison of the top `p` bits. Build a mask with `p` ones followed by `32 - p` zeros, AND it with both addresses and compare what is left.
hints: Convert both dotted strings to 32-bit integers first; strings cannot be compared bit by bit.
The mask for `/p` is `((1 << p) - 1) << (32 - p)`. Check it by hand for `/24` and `/0`.
Mask **both** sides: the block itself may have host bits set.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate every address in the block and test for equality. A `/8` has 16 million addresses, so this is O(2^(32-p)) and useless for large blocks.
guide.approach:
1. Parse the prefix length `p` and the base address.
2. `mask = ((1 << p) - 1) << (32 - p)`.
3. Return `(ip & mask) == (base & mask)`.

**Dry run:** `192.168.5.130` in `192.168.5.128/25`. The mask is `255.255.255.128`. Last octet of the address: `130 = 1000 0010`, AND `1000 0000` gives `128`. Last octet of the base: `128 & 128 = 128`. The first three octets are identical, so the masked values match → `True`. For `.127 = 0111 1111` the AND gives `0`, which differs from `128` → `False`.
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Comparing whole octets only works for /8, /16 and /24. In languages with 32-bit integers a shift by 32 is undefined, so `/0` needs care; Python integers are unbounded, which is why the mask is built by shifting left rather than by inverting.
guide.follow_up: Given many blocks, find the most specific one containing an address (see *Longest-Prefix-Match Routing*).

net-subnet-info.title: Subnet Mask, Network, Broadcast and Host Count

guide.prereqs: Problems *IPv4 Address and Integer Conversion* and *Is an Address Inside a CIDR Block?*.
guide.intuition: Everything falls out of one mask. AND with the mask clears the host bits (network); OR with the inverted mask sets them (broadcast); the number of host bits gives the block size.
hints: Compute the 32-bit mask first, exactly as in the CIDR membership problem.
The inverted mask (`mask ^ 0xFFFFFFFF`) has ones precisely in the host positions.
Handle `/31` and `/32` separately for the host count; the generic formula gives 0 and -1.
guide.brute_force: Work octet by octet with special cases for where the prefix boundary lands. It works but needs fiddly branching; the integer approach removes all of it.
guide.approach:
1. Convert the address to an integer `n` and build `mask`.
2. `network = n & mask`, `broadcast = network | ~mask` (restricted to 32 bits).
3. Hosts: `2^(32-p) - 2`, except 2 for `/31` and 1 for `/32`.
4. Convert the three integers back to dotted form.

**Dry run** `192.168.10.77/26`: host bits = 6, so the mask ends in `1100 0000 = 192`. `77 = 0100 1101`; AND `192` → `64`; OR `0011 1111` → `127`. Hosts `2^6 - 2 = 62`.
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: `~mask` in Python is a negative number; XOR with `0xFFFFFFFF` instead. The broadcast is not always `.255`. Forgetting the `/31` and `/32` special cases is the most common interview slip.
guide.follow_up: Return the first and last usable host, or decide whether two interface addresses are on the same subnet.

net-split-subnets.title: Split a Network into N Subnets
net-split-subnets.description:
You are given a block such as `"10.0.0.0/22"` and need at least `n` equal-sized subnets.

Borrow the **smallest** number of bits `k` such that `2^k >= n`, giving a new prefix length `p + k`,
and return **all** `2^k` resulting subnets in ascending address order as CIDR strings.

- Clear any host bits in the input block first (`"10.0.1.7/22"` is treated as `"10.0.0.0/22"`).
- `n >= 1`. For `n = 1` return the (normalised) block itself.
- If `p + k > 32` the split is impossible: return `[]`.

**Example:** `cidr = "192.168.0.0/24"`, `n = 3` → `["192.168.0.0/26", "192.168.0.64/26", "192.168.0.128/26", "192.168.0.192/26"]`
net-split-subnets.starter:
def split_network(cidr: str, n: int) -> list:
    pass
net-split-subnets.solution:
def split_network(cidr, n):
    addr, p = cidr.split("/")
    p = int(p)
    base = 0
    for part in addr.split("."):
        base = (base << 8) | int(part)
    base &= ((1 << p) - 1) << (32 - p)
    k = 0
    while (1 << k) < n:
        k += 1
    q = p + k
    if q > 32:
        return []
    step = 1 << (32 - q)
    out = []
    for i in range(1 << k):
        v = base + i * step
        out.append(".".join(str((v >> s) & 255) for s in (24, 16, 8, 0)) + "/" + str(q))
    return out

guide.prereqs: Problem *Subnet Mask, Network, Broadcast and Host Count*; powers of two.
guide.intuition: Each borrowed bit doubles the number of subnets and halves their size. Once you know the new prefix `q`, consecutive subnets are simply `2^(32-q)` addresses apart.
hints: How many bits do you need to count to `n` distinct values? That is `ceil(log2(n))`.
Avoid floating-point logs: loop `k` upward until `1 << k >= n`.
Subnet `i` starts at `base + i * 2^(32 - q)`; format each as dotted plus `/q`.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate every address in the block and group them by their top `q` bits. That is O(2^(32-p)) work for something that only needs O(2^k) outputs.
guide.approach:
1. Normalise the base address by masking with the original prefix.
2. Find the smallest `k` with `2^k >= n`; let `q = p + k`. If `q > 32`, return `[]`.
3. `step = 2^(32-q)`; emit `base + i*step` for `i = 0 .. 2^k - 1`.

**Dry run** `192.168.0.0/24`, `n = 3`: `k = 2` (4 ≥ 3), `q = 26`, `step = 64`. Subnets start at `.0`, `.64`, `.128`, `.192`.
guide.complexity: Time and space O(2^k), the size of the answer.
guide.pitfalls: `n.bit_length()` is off by one for exact powers of two (4 needs 2 bits, not 3). Returning only `n` subnets instead of all `2^k` leaves part of the block unaccounted for. Forgetting to clear host bits yields misaligned subnets.
guide.follow_up: Variable-length subnet masking: given a list of required host counts, allocate the smallest fitting block for each, largest first.

net-longest-prefix-match.title: Longest-Prefix-Match Routing
net-longest-prefix-match.description:
A router's forwarding table is a list of `[cidr, next_hop]` entries. To forward a packet it selects, among
all entries whose block contains the destination, the one with the **longest prefix** (the most specific).

Write `route_lookup(routes, destinations)` returning the chosen `next_hop` for every destination address.

- If no entry matches, the answer is `"unreachable"`.
- If two matching entries have the same prefix length, the one that appears **first** in `routes` wins.
- A `0.0.0.0/0` entry is a default route: it matches everything but loses to anything more specific.
- Entries may be written with host bits set; mask before comparing.

**Example:**
`routes = [["0.0.0.0/0","isp"], ["10.0.0.0/8","core"], ["10.1.0.0/16","dc1"], ["10.1.2.0/24","rack7"]]`,
`destinations = ["10.1.2.9", "10.1.9.9", "10.200.0.1", "8.8.8.8"]` → `["rack7", "dc1", "core", "isp"]`
net-longest-prefix-match.starter:
def route_lookup(routes: list, destinations: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Problem *Is an Address Inside a CIDR Block?*; hash maps; the lesson on routing.
guide.intuition: Several routes can match; specificity decides. Either scan every route and keep the longest match, or index routes by `(prefix length, masked network)` and probe from /32 downward, stopping at the first hit.
hints: Start with the simple scan: for each destination, test every route and remember the best prefix length seen so far.
Use a strict `>` when comparing prefix lengths so the earlier of two equal-length routes survives.
To go faster, store routes in a dict keyed by `(p, network)` and try the distinct prefix lengths in descending order.
guide.brute_force: For each destination test all `R` routes: O(D·R). Perfectly acceptable for small tables and a fine first answer in an interview.
guide.approach:
1. Pre-process: for each route compute `(p, base & mask)` and store the first next hop seen for that key.
2. Collect the distinct prefix lengths, sorted longest first.
3. For each destination, mask it with each length in turn and look the pair up; the first hit is the longest match.

**Dry run:** destination `10.1.9.9`. Try /24 → `10.1.9.0` not present. Try /16 → `10.1.0.0` present → `dc1`. We never reach /8 or /0.
guide.complexity: Pre-processing O(R). Each lookup probes at most 33 prefix lengths, so O(1) per destination with respect to table size; space O(R). Real routers use tries or TCAM hardware for the same job.
guide.pitfalls: Returning the first matching route (order-dependent, wrong). Using `>=` lets a later duplicate override an earlier one. Forgetting the default route must lose to every more specific entry.
guide.follow_up: Implement the lookup with a binary trie so that a lookup walks at most 32 nodes and supports route insertion and deletion.

net-internet-checksum.title: Internet Checksum
net-internet-checksum.description:
IPv4, ICMP, UDP and TCP all protect their headers with the same 16-bit ones' complement checksum (RFC 1071).

Given `data`, a list of byte values (0–255), compute it:

1. If the number of bytes is odd, append one zero byte.
2. Treat the bytes as big-endian 16-bit words and add them all.
3. While the sum does not fit in 16 bits, add the overflow (the bits above bit 15) back into the low 16 bits (end-around carry).
4. Return the bitwise complement of the result, as an integer in `[0, 65535]`.

An empty list returns `65535`.

**Example:** `[0x45, 0x00, 0x00, 0x1c]` → `0x4500 + 0x001c = 0x451c`, complement → `0xbae3 = 47843`

guide.prereqs: Hexadecimal, shifts and masks; the lesson on IPv6, ICMP and routing (IPv4 header layout).
guide.intuition: Ones' complement addition is ordinary addition where any carry out of the top bit wraps around and is added at the bottom. Sum the words in a big integer, fold the carries back, then flip the bits.
hints: Pair the bytes: word = `(high << 8) | low`. Pad a trailing odd byte with a zero **low** byte.
Do not truncate to 16 bits: the bits that overflow must be added back in.
One fold may itself overflow, so repeat `total = (total & 0xFFFF) + (total >> 16)` until nothing is left above bit 15.
guide.brute_force: Fold after every single addition. It gives the same result because end-around carry is associative, but it does more work than folding once at the end.
guide.approach:
1. Pad to an even length.
2. Add all 16-bit big-endian words into `total`.
3. Fold: while `total >> 16` is non-zero, `total = (total & 0xFFFF) + (total >> 16)`.
4. Return `total ^ 0xFFFF`.

**Dry run** `[0xFF,0xFF,0x00,0x01]`: sum `0xFFFF + 0x0001 = 0x10000`. Fold: `0x0000 + 0x1 = 0x0001`. Complement: `0xFFFE = 65534`. A receiver that sums the data **including** the checksum gets `0xFFFF`, which is how verification works (see the test where a correct IPv4 header returns 0).
guide.complexity: Time O(n) for n bytes, space O(1) extra.
guide.pitfalls: Masking with `& 0xFFFF` instead of folding throws the carries away. Padding at the front instead of the end shifts every word. Using Python's `~` yields a negative number; XOR with `0xFFFF`.
guide.follow_up: Incremental update (RFC 1624): when a router decrements the TTL it adjusts the checksum without re-summing the header. Why is this checksum weaker than a CRC?

net-mac-learning-switch.title: MAC Learning Switch
net-mac-learning-switch.description:
Simulate a transparent Ethernet switch with ports numbered `0 .. num_ports - 1` and an initially empty
MAC address table. Frames arrive one at a time as `[in_port, src_mac, dst_mac]`.

For each frame, in this order:

1. **Learn:** record that `src_mac` lives on `in_port` (overwriting any older entry: the host may have moved).
2. **Forward:**
   - if `dst_mac` is the broadcast address `"ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff"` or is not in the table, **flood**: send out of every port except `in_port`, in ascending order;
   - if `dst_mac` is in the table and its port equals `in_port`, **filter**: send nowhere (`[]`);
   - otherwise send out of the single learned port.

Return the list of output-port lists, one per frame. The broadcast address is never learned as a source.

**Example:** `num_ports = 3`, frames `[[0,"aa","bb"], [1,"bb","aa"], [0,"aa","bb"]]` → `[[1,2], [0], [1]]`
net-mac-learning-switch.starter:
def switch_sim(num_ports: int, frames: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Ethernet, MAC addresses, ARP and switching*; dictionaries.
guide.intuition: A switch never needs configuration: it learns where each station is by reading the **source** address of frames passing through, and uses that table to decide where frames for a **destination** go. Unknown means ask everyone.
hints: Keep a dict from MAC address to port. Which field of the frame updates it?
Learn first, then look up the destination, so a frame addressed to its own sender is filtered.
Three outcomes: flood (broadcast or unknown), filter (same port), forward (one port).
guide.brute_force: Flood every frame like a hub. It delivers correctly but wastes bandwidth and is exactly what the table exists to avoid; it also fails the tests that expect a single port.
guide.approach:
1. `table[src] = in_port` (skip the broadcast address).
2. If `dst` is broadcast or missing from the table, output all ports except `in_port`.
3. Else if `table[dst] == in_port`, output `[]`.
4. Else output `[table[dst]]`.

**Dry run** (3 ports): frame `[0,aa,bb]` learns aa→0; bb unknown → flood `[1,2]`. Frame `[1,bb,aa]` learns bb→1; aa known on 0 → `[0]`. Frame `[0,aa,bb]` → bb known on 1 → `[1]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(F·P) in the worst case (every frame floods to P ports); table operations are O(1) each. Space O(number of distinct MACs).
guide.pitfalls: Using `setdefault` so that a host which moves to another port is never updated. Forgetting to exclude the ingress port when flooding (causes loops in real networks). Forgetting the filter case when source and destination sit behind the same port.
guide.follow_up: Add an ageing timer so entries expire after 300 seconds, and VLAN tags so that flooding stays within one VLAN.

net-nat-table.title: NAT Translation Table
net-nat-table.description:
Simulate a home router performing port address translation (NAPT) with one public address.

`packets` is processed in order. Each packet is either

- `["out", src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port]`: a private host sends to the Internet, or
- `["in", src_ip, src_port, dst_port]`: an Internet host sends to the router's public address on `dst_port`.

**Outbound.** Each distinct private endpoint `(src_ip, src_port)` is given one public port, reused for every
destination. Ports are handed out in order: `first_port`, `first_port + 1`, … Mappings never expire.
The router also remembers that this private endpoint has contacted `(dst_ip, dst_port)`.
The result for the packet is the rewritten tuple `[public_ip, public_port, dst_ip, dst_port]`.

**Inbound.** If `dst_port` has a mapping **and** the mapped private endpoint has previously sent a packet to
exactly `(src_ip, src_port)`, the result is `[private_ip, private_port]` (where the packet is delivered).
Otherwise the result is the string `"drop"`.

Return the list of results.

**Example:** `public_ip = "203.0.113.5"`, `first_port = 40000`,
`packets = [["out","192.168.0.2",5555,"1.1.1.1",53], ["in","1.1.1.1",53,40000], ["in","9.9.9.9",53,40000]]`
→ `[["203.0.113.5",40000,"1.1.1.1",53], ["192.168.0.2",5555], "drop"]`
net-nat-table.starter:
def nat_sim(public_ip: str, first_port: int, packets: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *IPv4 addressing, subnets, CIDR and NAT*; dictionaries and sets.
guide.intuition: NAT is two dictionaries that are inverses of each other (private endpoint → public port, public port → private endpoint) plus a filter that only admits replies from peers the inside host has already spoken to.
hints: Key the outbound map by the pair `(private_ip, private_port)`, not by the IP alone.
Allocate a new public port only the first time an endpoint is seen; reuse it afterwards.
Store `(public_port, remote_ip, remote_port)` in a set on every outbound packet and consult it on every inbound one.
guide.brute_force: Keep a plain list of mappings and scan it for every packet: O(P·M). Dictionaries make each packet O(1).
guide.approach:
1. Outbound: look up or create the mapping, add the permitted remote endpoint, emit the rewritten 4-tuple.
2. Inbound: the packet is delivered only if the port maps to someone **and** the triple `(port, src_ip, src_port)` is permitted.

**Dry run:** `192.168.0.2:5555 → 1.1.1.1:53` allocates 40000 and permits `(40000, 1.1.1.1, 53)`. A reply from `1.1.1.1:53` to port 40000 is delivered to `192.168.0.2:5555`. A packet from `9.9.9.9:53` to the same port is dropped: nobody inside talked to it.
guide.complexity: Time O(P) for P packets, space O(number of mappings + permitted peers).
guide.pitfalls: Allocating a fresh port per packet instead of per endpoint. Forwarding any inbound packet that hits a mapped port (that is a *full-cone* NAT, not the port-restricted behaviour specified here). Mixing up which port an inbound packet is addressed to.
guide.follow_up: Add idle timeouts (e.g. 30 s for UDP, minutes for TCP) and explain why long-lived idle connections die behind NATs, and how keep-alives or STUN/TURN work around it.

net-traceroute-hops.title: Reconstruct a Traceroute Path
net-traceroute-hops.description:
Traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3, … Each router that decrements a probe's TTL to zero answers with an
ICMP *Time Exceeded* message, revealing its address; the destination itself answers the first probe that
reaches it.

You are given the collected `replies` in arbitrary order, each `[ttl, responder_ip, rtt_ms]`, and the
destination address `dest`. Several probes are sent per TTL; some get no reply; load balancing may make
different routers answer for the same TTL.

Build the path:

- Let `last` be the **smallest** TTL at which some reply came from `dest`; if `dest` never replied, `last` is the largest TTL present. With no replies at all, return `[]`.
- For each TTL from 1 to `last` output one hop `[ip, best_rtt]`:
  - `ip` is the responder seen most often at that TTL (ties → the lexicographically smallest string);
  - `best_rtt` is the minimum RTT among replies from that `ip` at that TTL;
  - a TTL with no replies yields `["*", -1]`.

**Example:** `replies = [[2,"10.0.0.1",9],[1,"192.168.1.1",2],[1,"192.168.1.1",1],[4,"93.184.216.34",30]]`, `dest = "93.184.216.34"`
→ `[["192.168.1.1",1], ["10.0.0.1",9], ["*",-1], ["93.184.216.34",30]]`
net-traceroute-hops.starter:
def reconstruct_path(replies: list, dest: str) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson on ping, traceroute, dig and curl; the IP TTL field and ICMP Time Exceeded; grouping with dictionaries.
guide.intuition: The TTL of the probe *is* the hop number, so group replies by TTL. Inside each group take a majority vote for the address. The path ends at the first TTL where the destination itself answers.
hints: Build `ttl -> {ip -> [rtts]}`.
Decide where the path stops before building it: the smallest TTL whose group contains `dest`, else the largest TTL seen.
Walk TTL 1..last **including** the missing ones, which become `["*", -1]`.
guide.brute_force: For each TTL rescan the whole reply list to count addresses: O(T·R). Grouping once makes it O(R).
guide.approach:
1. Group replies by TTL and then by responder.
2. `last = min(ttl where dest replied)` or `max(ttl)`.
3. For each TTL in `1..last`: missing → `["*", -1]`; otherwise pick the address with the most replies (ties by string order) and its minimum RTT.

**Dry run** (the example): TTL 1 → `192.168.1.1` twice, best RTT 1. TTL 2 → `10.0.0.1`, 9. TTL 3 → nothing → `*`. TTL 4 → the destination → stop.
guide.complexity: Time O(R + T) for R replies and T hops; space O(R).
guide.pitfalls: Continuing past the destination (later probes also reach it and would repeat it). Skipping silent hops instead of emitting `*`, which shifts every later hop number. Taking the minimum RTT over all responders rather than the chosen one.
guide.follow_up: Why can a later hop show a *lower* RTT than an earlier one? (ICMP generation is rate-limited and handled on a router's slow path; the return path may differ.)

net-dns-resolver.title: DNS Resolver with CNAME Chains and a TTL Cache
net-dns-resolver.description:
Simulate a caching resolver in front of an authoritative data set.

`records` is the authoritative data: `[name, type, ttl, value]` with `type` either `"A"` (value is an
address) or `"CNAME"` (value is another name). Each name has at most one record.

`queries` is a list of `[time, name]` with non-decreasing times (seconds). For each query, start at `name`
and repeat:

1. If the cache holds an entry for the current name with `time < expiry`, use it (no upstream lookup).
2. Otherwise perform one **upstream lookup**. If the name has no record, the answer is `"NXDOMAIN"`
   (negative answers are not cached). Otherwise store the record in the cache with `expiry = time + ttl`.
3. An `A` record ends the resolution with its address. A `CNAME` makes its value the current name;
   if this would be the **9th** CNAME followed for this query, stop with `"SERVFAIL"` instead (loop protection).

Return, for every query, `[answer, upstream_lookups]`.

**Example:** `records = [["www.a.test","CNAME",300,"a.test"], ["a.test","A",30,"192.0.2.1"]]`,
`queries = [[0,"www.a.test"], [10,"www.a.test"], [40,"www.a.test"]]`
→ `[["192.0.2.1",2], ["192.0.2.1",0], ["192.0.2.1",1]]`

(At time 40 the CNAME is still cached but the A record, cached at time 0 with TTL 30, has expired.)
net-dns-resolver.starter:
def resolve(records: list, queries: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lessons *How DNS resolution works* and *DNS caching, TTLs, anycast and failures*; dictionaries.
guide.intuition: Resolution is a walk along a linked list of names, where every step is either answered from memory or costs one upstream trip. Each link has its own lifetime, so a later query may reuse the first half of a chain and refetch only the part that expired.
hints: Cache per **name**, not per query: store `(type, value, expiry)`.
An entry is usable only while `time < expiry`; at exactly `expiry` it is stale.
Count CNAME hops inside one query and bail out with `SERVFAIL` when the count would exceed 8.
guide.brute_force: No cache at all: every query walks the whole chain upstream. Correct answers, but the lookup counts are wrong and in real life every page view would pay full resolution latency.
guide.approach:
1. Index the authoritative records by name.
2. For each query loop: cache hit → use it; miss → count a lookup, handle NXDOMAIN, store with expiry.
3. Stop on an A record; on a CNAME increment the hop count, check the limit, and continue with the target.

**Dry run** (example): t=0 misses `www.a.test` (lookup 1, cached until 300) and `a.test` (lookup 2, cached until 30). t=10: both cached → 0 lookups. t=40: CNAME cached, `a.test` expired (40 ≥ 30) → 1 lookup.
guide.complexity: Time O(chain length) per query, at most 9 steps; space O(number of names cached).
guide.pitfalls: Caching the final answer under the original name (ignores the shorter TTL further down the chain). Using `<=` for the expiry test. No loop protection: two CNAMEs pointing at each other spin forever. Caching NXDOMAIN when the specification says not to.
guide.follow_up: Add negative caching with the SOA minimum TTL, or cap every TTL at a resolver-chosen maximum and floor, as real resolvers do.

net-http-parse.title: Parse an HTTP/1.1 Message
net-http-parse.description:
Parse one well-formed HTTP/1.1 message given as a string `raw`. Lines of the head end with `\r\n` and the
head is separated from the body by an empty line (`\r\n\r\n`).

- If the start line begins with `HTTP/` it is a **response** `version status reason` (the reason phrase may
  contain spaces or be missing). Return `["response", version, status_as_int, reason, headers, body]`.
- Otherwise it is a **request** `method target version`. Return `["request", method, target, version, headers, body]`.

`headers` is a dict:

- split each header line at the **first** colon; lower-case the name; strip spaces and tabs around the value;
- if a name repeats, join the values with `", "` in order of appearance.

`body` is everything after the blank line; if a `content-length` header is present, keep only that many
characters. A message with no blank line has an empty body.

**Example:** `"GET /a?b=1 HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x.test:8080\r\n\r\n"` → `["request", "GET", "/a?b=1", "HTTP/1.1", {"host": "x.test:8080"}, ""]`

guide.prereqs: The lesson *From HTTP/0.9 to HTTP/1.1*: message structure, start line, headers, blank line, body.
guide.intuition: An HTTP/1.1 message is text with a rigid skeleton: one start line, zero or more `name: value` lines, a blank line, then opaque bytes. Split on the first blank line, then treat the head line by line.
hints: `str.partition` splits at the first occurrence only, which is what you want both for the blank line and for the header colon.
Decide request or response from the first five characters of the start line.
Split a status line with `split(' ', 2)` so a multi-word reason phrase stays in one piece.
guide.brute_force: Walk the string character by character with a hand-written state machine (as real parsers do for speed and safety). For well-formed input, a few `partition` and `split` calls say the same thing in a dozen lines.
guide.approach:
1. `head, _, body = raw.partition('\r\n\r\n')`.
2. First line of `head` is the start line; each remaining line is partitioned at its first `:`.
3. Normalise names to lower case, strip values, merge duplicates with `", "`.
4. Truncate the body to `content-length` when given.
5. Build the request or response list.

**Dry run:** `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found` → `split(' ', 2)` → `['HTTP/1.1', '404', 'Not Found']`. Header `Host: x.test:8080` partitions into `Host` and ` x.test:8080`; a naive `split(':')` would lose the port.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) in the message length; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Splitting header lines on every colon (breaks URLs, times and host:port). Splitting the status line on every space (truncates `Not Found`). Treating header names as case-sensitive. Splitting the whole message on `\r\n`, which corrupts bodies containing blank lines.
guide.follow_up: Handle `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` (next problem), reject messages with both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` (request smuggling), and parse incrementally from a byte stream.

net-chunked-decode.title: Decode Chunked Transfer Encoding
net-chunked-decode.description:
With `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` an HTTP/1.1 body is sent as a series of chunks so the sender need not know
the total length in advance:

```
<size in hexadecimal>[;extensions]\r\n
<exactly size characters of data>\r\n
...
0\r\n
[optional trailer header lines]\r\n
```

Given the encoded body `data` (well-formed), return the decoded payload.

- The size may use upper- or lower-case hex digits; ignore anything after a `;` on the size line.
- Chunk data can contain any characters, **including `\r\n`**; only the declared size tells you where it ends.
- Stop at the zero-size chunk; ignore trailers.

**Example:** `"4\r\nWiki\r\n5\r\npedia\r\n0\r\n\r\n"` → `"Wikipedia"`

guide.prereqs: The lesson *From HTTP/0.9 to HTTP/1.1* (message framing); hexadecimal.
guide.intuition: This is length-prefixed framing. Read a length, read exactly that many characters, skip the trailing CRLF, repeat. The data is never inspected for delimiters.
hints: Keep a cursor index into the string instead of splitting it.
`int(text, 16)` parses the size; cut off extensions with `split(';')[0]` first.
After copying `size` characters, advance by `size + 2` to skip the CRLF that follows the data.
guide.brute_force: Split the whole body on `\r\n` and take every second piece. It passes simple cases but breaks as soon as a chunk's data contains a line break, because it trusts delimiters rather than lengths.
guide.approach:
1. `i = 0`. Find the next `
` from `i`; the text before it is the size line.
2. Parse the hex size. Zero → done.
3. Append `data[i : i+size]`, move `i` past the data and its CRLF.

**Dry run** `"4
Wiki
5
pedia
0

"`: size 4 → `Wiki`, cursor to 9. Size 5 → `pedia`, cursor to 19. Size 0 → stop. Result `Wikipedia`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the output.
guide.pitfalls: Parsing the size as decimal (`10` means sixteen). Searching the data for CRLF. Forgetting chunk extensions. Stopping at an empty data segment instead of at a zero **size**.
guide.follow_up: Write the encoder, and a streaming decoder that accepts input in arbitrary pieces (a chunk header may be split across two reads).

net-cache-freshness.title: Cache-Control Freshness Decision
net-cache-freshness.description:
Decide what an HTTP cache may do with a stored response. Inputs:

- `headers`: a dict that may contain `"cache-control"` (a string of comma-separated directives) and the
  integers `"date"` and `"expires"` (already converted to epoch seconds);
- `age`: how many seconds the response has been in caches;
- `shared`: `True` for a shared cache (CDN, proxy), `False` for a private browser cache.

Directive names are case-insensitive and may be surrounded by spaces; some carry `=number`.
Apply these rules **in order** and return the first result that applies:

1. `no-store` present → `"no-store"`.
2. `private` present and the cache is shared → `"no-store"`.
3. `no-cache` present → `"revalidate"`.
4. Compute the freshness lifetime: for a shared cache with `s-maxage`, that value; otherwise `max-age` if
   present; otherwise `max(0, expires - date)` if both keys exist; otherwise `0`.
5. `age < lifetime` → `"fresh"`.
6. `must-revalidate` present, or `proxy-revalidate` present and the cache is shared → `"revalidate"`.
7. `stale-while-revalidate=N` present and `age < lifetime + N` → `"stale-while-revalidate"`.
8. Otherwise → `"revalidate"`.

**Example:** `headers = {"cache-control": "public, max-age=600"}`, `age = 120`, `shared = False` → `"fresh"`

**Example:** `headers = {"cache-control": "max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30"}`, `age = 75`, `shared = True` → `"stale-while-revalidate"`

def cache_decision(headers: dict, age: int, shared: bool) -> str:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *HTTP caching, cookies and content negotiation*: Cache-Control directives, freshness lifetime, validation.
guide.intuition: A cache asks three questions in order: am I allowed to keep this at all, how long is it good for, and if it has gone off, how strict is the origin about serving it anyway? The rule list is that conversation written down.
hints: Parse the directive string into a dict first; flags map to an empty string, valued directives to their number.
The lifetime has a strict priority: `s-maxage` (shared only), then `max-age`, then `Expires − Date`.
`must-revalidate` is checked before `stale-while-revalidate`: it forbids serving stale content.
guide.brute_force: Chains of `if 'max-age' in header_string` substring tests. They break on case differences, on `s-maxage` containing the text `maxage`, and on spacing; a single tokenising pass removes all of that.
guide.approach:
1. Tokenise: split on commas, trim, lower-case, partition on `=`.
2. Walk rules 1–8 in order, returning at the first match.

**Dry run** `max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30`, age 75, shared: not `no-store`, not `private`, not `no-cache`. Lifetime 60. `75 < 60` false → not fresh. No `must-revalidate`. `75 < 60 + 30` → `"stale-while-revalidate"`: serve the stored copy now and refresh it in the background.
guide.complexity: Time O(d) in the number of directives; space O(d).
guide.pitfalls: Giving `max-age` priority over `s-maxage` in a shared cache. Treating `no-cache` as 'do not store' (it means 'store, but revalidate before every use'). Using `<=` for freshness. Treating `private` as uncacheable in the browser.
guide.follow_up: Add the `Age` header arithmetic, heuristic freshness (10% of the time since `Last-Modified`), and request directives such as `max-stale` and `only-if-cached`.

net-cookie-match.title: Cookie Jar: Which Cookies Are Sent?
net-cookie-match.description:
Implement a small cookie jar. `set_cookies` is a list of `[host, header]` pairs: the `Set-Cookie` header
value received in a response from `host`, in chronological order. Afterwards a request
`[scheme, host, path]` is made; return the exact `Cookie` header value to send (or `""`).

**Storing.** Split the header on `;`. The first piece is `name=value` (split at the first `=`, trim both).
The remaining pieces are attributes with case-insensitive names:

- `Domain=d`: drop one leading `.` and lower-case. If the responding host is neither equal to `d` nor ends
  with `"." + d`, **ignore the whole cookie**. Without a (non-empty) Domain attribute the cookie is *host-only*
  and its domain is the responding host.
- `Path=p`: used if it starts with `/`; otherwise (or if absent) the path is `/`.
- `Secure`: flag.
- `Max-Age=n` (an integer): if `n <= 0` the cookie is a **deletion**.
- Anything else (HttpOnly, SameSite, …) is ignored.

A cookie's identity is `(name, domain, path)`. Storing a cookie with an existing identity replaces the value
and flags but **keeps the original creation order**. A deletion removes the cookie with that identity (if any)
and stores nothing.

**Sending.** A stored cookie is sent when all hold:

- host: host-only cookies need `request host == domain`; others need equality or the request host ending in `"." + domain`;
- path: the request path equals the cookie path, or starts with it and either the cookie path ends in `/` or the
  next character of the request path is `/`;
- `Secure` cookies need scheme `https`.

Order: longer cookie paths first; ties by earlier creation. Join as `name=value` with `"; "`.
Hosts compare case-insensitively.

**Example:** `set_cookies = [["shop.test", "sid=abc; Path=/; Secure"], ["shop.test", "theme=dark; Path=/account"]]`,
`request = ["https", "shop.test", "/account/orders"]` → `"theme=dark; sid=abc"`
net-cookie-match.starter:
def cookies_to_send(set_cookies: list, request: list) -> str:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *HTTP caching, cookies and content negotiation*: Set-Cookie attributes, domain and path scoping.
guide.intuition: A cookie is a small record with a scope (domain, path, secure) and an identity (name, domain, path). Storing is upsert-or-delete by identity; sending is a filter by scope followed by a sort.
hints: Parse each header into a record first; keep parsing and matching as two separate phases.
Domain matching needs a dot boundary: `badshop.test` must not match `shop.test`. Path matching needs a slash boundary: `/apple` must not match `/app`.
Use a dict keyed by `(name, domain, path)` holding a creation counter that is assigned once and preserved on replacement.
guide.brute_force: Store every header in a list and, at request time, re-parse them all and resolve replacements by scanning backwards. O(n²) and easy to get wrong; a keyed jar makes replacement and deletion one dictionary operation.
guide.approach:
1. For each `Set-Cookie`: parse name/value and attributes; determine host-only vs domain cookie; reject foreign domains; upsert or delete by identity.
2. For the request: keep cookies whose host rule, path rule and secure rule all pass.
3. Sort by `(-len(path), creation)` and join.

**Dry run** (example): `sid` is stored host-only for `shop.test`, path `/`, secure, creation 0; `theme` with path `/account`, creation 1. Request `https://shop.test/account/orders`: both hosts match; `/account/orders` starts with `/account` and the next character is `/` ✓; `/` matches everything ✓. Longer path first → `theme=dark; sid=abc`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) to store and O(m log m) to select m matching cookies; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Plain `endswith(domain)` and `startswith(path)` are the classic security bugs. A host-only cookie must not be sent to subdomains. Replacement must not change ordering. A value may itself contain `=`. `Max-Age=0` is how servers delete cookies.
guide.follow_up: Add `Expires`, the `SameSite` rules for cross-site requests, the `__Host-` prefix requirements, and public-suffix checks (a site must not set a cookie for `.com`).

net-url-normalize.title: URL Parsing and Normalisation
net-url-normalize.description:
Caches, crawlers and routers need to recognise that two differently written URLs are the same resource.
Normalise an absolute `http` or `https` URL of the form

`scheme://host[:port][/path][?query][#fragment]`

by applying exactly these steps:

1. Remove the fragment (`#` and everything after it).
2. Lower-case the scheme and the host.
3. Remove the port if it is the scheme's default (`80` for http, `443` for https).
4. In the path and in the query, fix percent-escapes: write the two hex digits in **upper case**, and
   **decode** the escape if it stands for an unreserved character (`A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~`). Leave everything else alone.
5. Remove dot segments from the path: split it on `/`; a `.` segment is dropped; a `..` segment removes the
   previous segment (if any). If the **last** segment was `.` or `..`, the path ends with `/`. Other empty
   segments are kept as they are.
6. An empty path becomes `/`.
7. Keep the query (after step 4) exactly as is; if it is empty, drop the `?`.

Return `scheme://host[:port]path[?query]`. Percent-escapes in the input are always well formed.

**Example:** `"HTTP://Example.TEST:80/a/./b/../c?x=1#top"` → `"http://example.test/a/c?x=1"`

**Example:** `"https://example.test/%7euser/%2fetc"` → `"https://example.test/~user/%2Fetc"`

guide.prereqs: URL anatomy (see *What happens when you type a URL*); percent-encoding; stacks.
guide.intuition: Peel the URL apart from the outside in (fragment, scheme, authority, path, query), normalise each piece by its own rules, and glue it back. Dot-segment removal is a stack: `..` pops.
hints: Remove the fragment first; then the authority ends at the first `/` **or** `?`, whichever comes first.
Only the scheme and host are case-insensitive. Never lower-case the path or query.
For dot segments, push normal segments on a list, pop on `..`, and remember to leave a trailing slash when the final segment was a dot segment.
guide.brute_force: Repeated string replacement (`replace('/./', '/')`, regexes for `/x/../`) until nothing changes. It is quadratic and mishandles edge cases such as leading `..` and trailing dots; a single stack pass is linear and exact.
guide.approach:
1. Strip the fragment; split off the scheme at `://`.
2. Cut the authority at the first `/` or `?`; split host and port; drop a default port.
3. Normalise percent-escapes in path and query.
4. Run the segment stack over the path.
5. Reassemble, omitting an empty query.

**Dry run** `/a/./b/../c`: segments `a . b .. c` → push a; skip `.`; push b; `..` pops b; push c → `/a/c`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Lower-casing the entire URL. Decoding reserved escapes such as `%2F` (changes the meaning: it is data, not a separator). Decoding escapes before splitting would also be wrong. Missing the case where the query appears with no path (`http://h?x=1`). Removing a non-default port.
guide.follow_up: Sort query parameters, strip tracking parameters, handle IDN hosts with punycode and IPv6 literals in brackets.

net-hpack-toy.title: HPACK-Style Header Table Indexing
net-hpack-toy.description:
HTTP/2 compresses headers by referring to entries in a table shared by encoder and decoder. Implement the
encoder for this simplified scheme.

**Static table** (fixed):

| index | name | value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `:method` | `GET` |
| 2 | `:method` | `POST` |
| 3 | `:path` | `/` |
| 4 | `:scheme` | `https` |
| 5 | `:status` | `200` |
| 6 | `accept-encoding` | `gzip, deflate` |
| 7 | `content-type` | *(empty)* |
| 8 | `user-agent` | *(empty)* |

**Dynamic table.** Starts empty and holds at most `max_entries` entries. New entries are inserted at the
**front**: the newest dynamic entry always has index 9, the next newest 10, and so on. When the table is
over capacity the oldest entry is evicted. With `max_entries = 0` nothing is ever stored.

`headers` is the list of `[name, value]` pairs sent on one connection, in order (possibly several requests
one after another). For each header, search static then dynamic entries in index order:

- if some entry matches both name and value, emit `["I", index]` using the **lowest** such index; the table does not change;
- otherwise, if some entry matches the name, emit `["N", lowest_name_index, value]`;
- otherwise emit `["L", name, value]`.

In the last two cases, insert `(name, value)` into the dynamic table **after** emitting.

Return the list of emitted items.

**Example:** `headers = [[":method","GET"], [":path","/cart"], [":path","/cart"]]`, `max_entries = 4`
→ `[["I",1], ["N",3,"/cart"], ["I",9]]`
net-hpack-toy.starter:
def hpack_encode(headers: list, max_entries: int) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *HTTP/2: streams, multiplexing and HPACK*.
guide.intuition: Most headers repeat from one request to the next. If both ends remember what was sent, a repeated header shrinks to a small number. The only subtlety is the numbering: new entries push older ones to higher indices, like a stack of plates with the newest on top.
hints: Model the dynamic table as a list with the newest entry at position 0; index = 9 + position.
Search before you insert: the header being encoded cannot refer to itself.
Stop at the first full match, but remember the first name-only match on the way in case no full match exists.
guide.brute_force: Send every header literally (`["L", name, value]`). Always decodable, zero compression: this is what HTTP/1.1 does, and why its header overhead is hundreds of bytes per request.
guide.approach:
1. For each header scan `STATIC + dynamic` with indices starting at 1, recording the first name match and stopping at the first full match.
2. Emit `I`, `N` or `L` accordingly.
3. For `N` and `L`, insert at the front and trim the list to `max_entries`.

**Dry run** (example): `:method GET` is static entry 1 → `["I",1]`. `:path /cart`: name matches static 3, no full match → `["N",3,"/cart"]`, table becomes `[(:path,/cart)]`. Again `:path /cart`: static 3 matches the name only; dynamic index 9 matches fully → `["I",9]`.
guide.complexity: Time O(h·(S + max_entries)) with a linear scan; real encoders keep hash maps for O(1) lookups. Space O(max_entries).
guide.pitfalls: Appending to the end of the dynamic table (indices then point at the wrong entries after the first eviction, and the decoder desynchronises). Inserting on an indexed hit. Forgetting `max_entries = 0`. Returning the first *name* match when a later *full* match exists.
guide.follow_up: Real HPACK measures the table in bytes (name + value + 32 per entry), Huffman-codes strings, and has a never-indexed form for secrets. QPACK (HTTP/3) changes the design so a lost packet cannot stall header decoding.

net-websocket-frame.title: Decode a WebSocket Frame
net-websocket-frame.description:
Decode one WebSocket frame (RFC 6455) from `data`, a list of byte values. Layout:

```
byte 0:  FIN (bit 7) | RSV1-3 (bits 6-4, ignore) | opcode (bits 3-0)
byte 1:  MASK (bit 7) | payload length indicator (bits 6-0)
         indicator 0-125 : that is the payload length
         indicator 126   : the next 2 bytes hold the length (big-endian)
         indicator 127   : the next 8 bytes hold the length (big-endian)
then:    4-byte masking key, only if MASK is set
then:    the payload
```

If MASK is set, the real payload byte `i` is `payload[i] XOR key[i % 4]`.

Return `[fin, opcode, masked, payload_length, payload]` where `fin` and `masked` are booleans and `payload`
is the list of **unmasked** byte values. If `data` is too short to contain the complete frame, return `[]`.
Bytes after the end of the frame are ignored.

**Example:** `[0x81, 0x02, 0x48, 0x69]` → `[True, 1, False, 2, [72, 105]]` (an unmasked text frame "Hi")

guide.prereqs: The lesson *WebSocket, WebRTC and choosing a transport*; bit masks and XOR.
guide.intuition: The header is variable-length, so decode it as a cursor walk: fixed two bytes, then an optional extended length, then an optional key, then the payload. At every step check that enough bytes remain before reading them.
hints: `byte & 0x80` tests the top bit; `byte & 0x0F` and `byte & 0x7F` extract the low fields.
Keep a `pos` variable for where the next field starts; the 126 and 127 cases move it to 4 and 10.
Unmask with `payload[i] ^ key[i % 4]`. XOR is its own inverse, so masking and unmasking are the same operation.
guide.brute_force: Write three separate decoders for the three length encodings, each duplicated for masked and unmasked frames. Six code paths; the cursor approach has one.
guide.approach:
1. Need at least 2 bytes. Extract FIN, opcode, MASK, 7-bit length.
2. Extended length: 126 → 2 bytes, 127 → 8 bytes, big-endian.
3. If masked, read the 4-byte key.
4. Check that the payload is fully present, slice it, unmask if needed.

**Dry run** `81 85 37 fa 21 3d 7f 9f 4d 51 58`: `0x81` → FIN, opcode 1 (text). `0x85` → masked, length 5. Key `37 fa 21 3d`. Payload `7f^37=48 'H'`, `9f^fa=65 'e'`, `4d^21=6c 'l'`, `51^3d=6c 'l'`, `58^37=6f 'o'` → "Hello".
guide.complexity: Time O(n) in the payload length; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls: Treating 126/127 as actual lengths. Reading the key before the extended length. Forgetting to unmask (client-to-server frames are always masked; server-to-client never). Indexing past the end on truncated input instead of returning `[]`.
guide.follow_up: Reassemble fragmented messages (FIN = 0 followed by continuation frames, opcode 0), and handle interleaved control frames (ping 0x9, pong 0xA, close 0x8).

net-lb-weighted-round-robin.title: Smooth Weighted Round-Robin Load Balancer
net-lb-weighted-round-robin.description:
A load balancer spreads requests over backends in proportion to integer `weights` (backend `i` has weight
`weights[i] >= 0`; at least one weight is positive unless the list is empty). Plain weighted round-robin
would send bursts (`A A A A A B`); the *smooth* variant used by nginx interleaves them.

Every backend has a running value `current`, initially 0. For each request:

1. add each backend's weight to its `current`;
2. pick the backend with the largest `current` (ties → the lowest index);
3. subtract the **sum of all weights** from the chosen backend's `current`.

Return the list of chosen backend indices for `n` requests. With an empty `weights` list return `[]`.
With all weights equal this is ordinary round-robin.

**Example:** `weights = [5, 1, 1]`, `n = 7` → `[0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 0]`
net-lb-weighted-round-robin.starter:
def weighted_round_robin(weights: list, n: int) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Load balancers, reverse proxies and health checks*.
guide.intuition: Think of `current` as accumulated credit. Everyone earns credit at their own rate each turn; whoever has the most gets served and pays the whole pot back. Heavy backends earn fast so they are served often, but paying the pot stops them being served many times in a row.
hints: You need one integer of state per backend plus the total weight.
Do the 'add weight' step for **all** backends before choosing.
Break ties towards the lowest index by using a strict `>` while scanning left to right.
guide.brute_force: Expand the weights into a repeating list (`[0,0,0,0,0,1,2]`) and cycle through it. The proportions are right but the order is bursty and does not match the specification; memory also grows with the weights.
guide.approach:
1. `total = sum(weights)`, `current = [0]*k`.
2. Per request: add weights, find the arg-max, subtract `total`, record.

**Dry run** `[5,1,1]`, total 7:

| request | current after adding | chosen | current after subtracting |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5, 1, 1 | 0 | -2, 1, 1 |
| 2 | 3, 2, 2 | 0 | -4, 2, 2 |
| 3 | 1, 3, 3 | 1 | 1, -4, 3 |
| 4 | 6, -3, 4 | 0 | -1, -3, 4 |
| 5 | 4, -2, 5 | 2 | 4, -2, -2 |
| 6 | 9, -1, -1 | 0 | 2, -1, -1 |
| 7 | 7, 0, 0 | 0 | 0, 0, 0 |

After `total` requests every `current` is back to 0 and the pattern repeats.
guide.complexity: Time O(n·k) for k backends; space O(k).
guide.pitfalls: Subtracting the backend's own weight rather than the total. Choosing before all credits are added. Using `>=`, which sends ties to the highest index. A zero-weight backend must never be chosen.
guide.follow_up: Combine with health checks (skip unhealthy backends and exclude their weight from the total) or with slow-start, where a newly added backend's effective weight ramps up.

net-lb-least-connections.title: Least-Connections Load Balancer with Health State
net-lb-least-connections.description:
Simulate a least-connections balancer over servers `0 .. num_servers - 1`, all initially healthy with zero
active connections. `events` are processed in order:

- `["req", id]`: a new request with a unique `id`. Assign it to the **healthy** server with the fewest active
  connections (ties → lowest index); that server's count rises by one. If no server is healthy the request is
  rejected with `-1` and occupies nothing.
- `["done", id]`: the request finishes; its server's count drops by one. Ignore ids that were rejected,
  already finished, or never seen.
- `["down", s]` / `["up", s]`: server `s` fails or passes its health check. A down server receives no new
  requests, but its existing connections stay counted until they finish.

Return the list of results for the `"req"` events only (server index or `-1`), in order.

**Example:** `num_servers = 2`, `events = [["req",1],["req",2],["req",3],["done",1],["req",4]]` → `[0, 1, 0, 0]`
net-lb-least-connections.starter:
def least_connections(num_servers: int, events: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Load balancers, reverse proxies and health checks*; dictionaries.
guide.intuition: Round-robin assumes every request costs the same. When some requests are slow, the fair thing is to look at who is busiest right now. So the balancer tracks open connections per server and a map from request to server so it knows whose count to decrement.
hints: Three pieces of state: `active[s]`, `healthy[s]`, and `request id -> server`.
Remove the id from the map when it completes so a duplicate `done` is harmless.
A server going down does not reset its count: those connections are still draining.
guide.brute_force: On every request recount each server's active connections by scanning the list of all open requests: O(R) per request. Keeping the counters up to date makes each event O(k) for k servers.
guide.approach:
1. `req`: scan the healthy servers for the minimum count (strict `<` keeps the lowest index on ties); record and increment.
2. `done`: pop the id from the map and decrement that server.
3. `down` / `up`: flip the flag only.

**Dry run** (example): req 1 → server 0 (0,0 → 1,0). req 2 → server 1 (1,1). req 3 → tie → server 0 (2,1). done 1 → (1,1). req 4 → tie → server 0.
guide.complexity: Time O(E·k) with a linear scan (a heap keyed by `(active, index)` gives O(log k) per event); space O(k + open requests).
guide.pitfalls: Decrementing twice for a repeated `done`. Zeroing the count of a failed server (it then looks idle the moment it recovers and gets flooded). Counting rejected requests. Forgetting the lowest-index tie-break.
guide.follow_up: Power of two choices: pick two random servers and use the less loaded one. It achieves nearly the same balance with O(1) work and no global scan, and avoids the herd effect when many balancers share stale load data.

net-consistent-hash.title: Consistent-Hash Ring Lookup
net-consistent-hash.description:
Map keys to servers with a consistent-hash ring so that adding or removing one server only moves a small
share of the keys.

Use the 32-bit **FNV-1a** hash, defined as

```
h = 2166136261
for each byte b of the UTF-8 encoding of the string:
    h = h XOR b
    h = (h * 16777619) mod 2^32
```

**Ring.** Every server `s` is placed on the ring `replicas` times, at positions
`fnv(s + "#" + str(i))` for `i = 0 .. replicas - 1` (virtual nodes).

**Lookup.** A key `k` belongs to the virtual node with the smallest position that is `>= fnv(k)`; if there
is none, wrap around to the virtual node with the smallest position overall. If two virtual nodes share a
position, the one whose server name is alphabetically smaller comes first.

Return the server name for each key in `keys`. If `servers` is empty return `""` for every key.

**Example:** `servers = ["a", "b"]`, `replicas = 1`, `keys = ["x"]`:
`fnv("a#0") = 4037809751`, `fnv("b#0") = 559601318`, `fnv("x") = 4245442695`. No position is `>=` the key's
hash, so wrap to the smallest position → `["b"]`.
net-consistent-hash.starter:
def consistent_hash(servers: list, replicas: int, keys: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: Hashing, binary search (`bisect`); the lesson *Load balancers, reverse proxies and health checks*.
guide.intuition: With `hash(key) % N`, changing N reshuffles almost every key. Instead, hash servers and keys onto the same circle and give each key to the next server clockwise. Removing a server only hands its arc to its neighbour. Virtual nodes cut each server's territory into many small arcs so the load evens out.
hints: Build a sorted list of `(position, server)` tuples once.
`bisect_left(ring, (h, ""))` finds the first tuple whose position is at least `h`, because the empty string sorts before every name.
If the index equals `len(ring)`, wrap to index 0.
guide.brute_force: For each key scan every virtual node to find the smallest position ≥ the hash: O(K·S·R). Sorting once and binary searching gives O(log(S·R)) per key.
guide.approach:
1. Implement FNV-1a exactly (XOR first, then multiply, masking to 32 bits).
2. `ring = sorted((fnv(f"{s}#{i}"), s) ...)`.
3. For each key: `idx = bisect_left(ring, (fnv(key), ""))`, wrap, answer `ring[idx][1]`.

**Dry run** (example): ring = `[(559601318, "b"), (4037809751, "a")]`. `fnv("x") = 4245442695` is beyond both, `idx = 2 = len(ring)` → wrap to 0 → `"b"`.
guide.complexity: Build O(S·R·log(S·R)); each lookup O(L + log(S·R)) for a key of length L; space O(S·R).
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting the wrap-around (index error or wrong owner for high hashes). Multiplying before XOR-ing gives FNV-1, a different function. Forgetting the 32-bit mask. Falling back to modulo hashing, which defeats the purpose.
guide.follow_up: Measure how many keys move when a server is added (compare the 4-server and 5-server tests). Look at bounded-load consistent hashing, rendezvous hashing and Maglev hashing as alternatives.

net-token-bucket.title: Token-Bucket Rate Limiter
net-token-bucket.description:
Implement a token-bucket limiter with explicit timestamps.

The bucket holds at most `capacity` tokens and starts **full** at time 0. Tokens are added continuously at
`rate` tokens per second, i.e. `rate * dt / 1000` tokens over `dt` milliseconds (fractions count), never
exceeding `capacity`.

`requests` is a list of `[t_ms, cost]` with non-decreasing integer timestamps. For each request:

1. refill for the time elapsed since the previous request (or since time 0);
2. if the bucket holds at least `cost` tokens, remove them and allow the request (`True`);
3. otherwise deny it (`False`) and remove nothing.

Return the list of booleans. `capacity`, `rate` and `cost` are non-negative integers.

**Hint on precision:** count in thousandths of a token (`rate * dt` milli-tokens per `dt` ms) so that all
arithmetic stays in integers.

**Example:** `capacity = 3`, `rate = 1`, `requests = [[0,1],[0,1],[0,1],[0,1],[500,1],[1000,1]]`
→ `[True, True, True, False, False, True]`
net-token-bucket.starter:
def token_bucket(capacity: int, rate: int, requests: list) -> list:
    pass
net-token-bucket.solution:
def token_bucket(capacity, rate, requests):
    cap = capacity * 1000
    tokens = cap
    last = 0
    out = []
    for t, cost in requests:
        tokens = min(cap, tokens + (t - last) * rate)
        last = t
        need = cost * 1000
        if tokens >= need:
            tokens -= need
            out.append(True)
        else:
            out.append(False)
    return out

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Timeouts, retries, pools, rate limits and idempotency*.
guide.intuition: Tokens are permission slips that drip into a bucket at the sustained rate. A full bucket lets a client burst; an empty one makes it wait for the drip. You never need a timer: when a request arrives, work out how many tokens *would* have dripped in since last time.
hints: Lazy refill: `tokens += elapsed * rate`, then clamp to `capacity`.
Update `last` on **every** request, allowed or denied, since the refill has been applied either way.
Work in milli-tokens (multiply capacity and cost by 1000) to avoid floating-point comparisons.
guide.brute_force: Advance a simulated clock one millisecond at a time, adding `rate/1000` tokens per tick. Time proportional to the timestamp range rather than the number of requests, and floating-point drift creeps in.
guide.approach:
1. `tokens = capacity·1000`, `last = 0`.
2. Per request: `tokens = min(cap, tokens + (t − last)·rate)`, `last = t`; compare with `cost·1000`.

**Dry run** `capacity 3, rate 1`: three requests at t=0 drain 3000 → 0. Fourth at t=0: 0 < 1000 → deny. t=500: +500 → 500 < 1000 → deny (the 500 stays). t=1000: +500 → 1000 → allow.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) besides the output.
guide.pitfalls: Not capping at capacity (a quiet period then permits an unbounded burst). Integer-dividing the refill each time, which throws away fractions of a token and under-serves steady clients. Charging tokens for denied requests. Starting the bucket empty.
guide.follow_up: Per-client buckets in a dict with idle eviction; a distributed version in Redis with an atomic script; returning a `Retry-After` value computed from the token deficit.

net-leaky-bucket.title: Leaky-Bucket Traffic Shaper
net-leaky-bucket.description:
A leaky-bucket shaper smooths bursts: packets wait in a bounded queue and leave at a steady pace, at most one
every `interval` milliseconds.

`arrivals` is a non-decreasing list of arrival times (ms). Process packets in order. For a packet arriving
at time `t`:

- its earliest possible departure is `d = t` if no packet has been accepted yet, otherwise
  `d = max(t, last_departure + interval)` where `last_departure` is the departure time of the most recently
  accepted packet;
- let `waiting` be the number of accepted packets whose departure time is **greater than** `t` (still queued);
- if `d > t` (the packet must wait) and `waiting >= queue_size`, the packet is **dropped**: record `-1`;
- otherwise it is accepted and departs at `d`: record `d`.

Return the list of recorded values.

**Example:** `queue_size = 2`, `interval = 100`, `arrivals = [0, 0, 0, 0, 250]` → `[0, 100, 200, -1, 300]`
net-leaky-bucket.starter:
def leaky_bucket(queue_size: int, interval: int, arrivals: list) -> list:
    pass
net-leaky-bucket.solution:
def leaky_bucket(queue_size, interval, arrivals):
    queued = collections.deque()
    last = None
    out = []
    for t in arrivals:
        while queued and queued[0] <= t:
            queued.popleft()
        d = t if last is None else max(t, last + interval)
        if d > t and len(queued) >= queue_size:
            out.append(-1)
            continue
        last = d
        queued.append(d)
        out.append(d)
    return out

guide.prereqs: Problem *Token-Bucket Rate Limiter*; queues (`collections.deque`).
guide.intuition: Where a token bucket lets bursts through, a leaky bucket irons them flat: output is a metronome. Each accepted packet reserves the next free tick; the queue bound limits how far into the future reservations may stretch.
hints: The departure time of a packet depends only on the previous accepted packet's departure time.
Before judging a new packet, discard queued departures that are `<= t`: those packets have left.
A packet that can leave immediately (`d == t`) never needs a queue slot, even when `queue_size` is 0.
guide.brute_force: Keep a list of all accepted departure times and count those greater than `t` for every arrival: O(n²). Because departures are increasing, a deque that drops expired entries from the front gives amortised O(1).
guide.approach:
1. Pop departures `<= t` from the front of the deque.
2. Compute `d`.
3. If the packet must wait and the queue is full, drop; otherwise record `d`, append it, and update `last`.

**Dry run** `queue 2, interval 100, arrivals 0,0,0,0,250`: first leaves at 0. Second: d=100, waiting 0 → accept. Third: d=200, waiting 1 → accept. Fourth: d=300, waiting 2 ≥ 2 → drop. At 250 the departures at 0, 100, 200 are gone; d = max(250, 300) = 300, waiting 0 → accept.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) amortised, space O(queue_size).
guide.pitfalls: Advancing `last` for a dropped packet (it reserved nothing). Counting the packet currently departing as waiting. Dropping a packet that could leave at once because the queue size is zero. Confusing this with the token bucket: the leaky bucket never emits two packets closer than `interval`.
guide.follow_up: Implement the leaky bucket *as a meter* (a counter that drains at a constant rate and rejects when it would overflow) and show it is equivalent to a token bucket with the same capacity.

net-backoff-jitter.title: Exponential Backoff Schedule with Jitter
net-backoff-jitter.description:
Compute the delays (in milliseconds) a client waits before each of `attempts` retries.

For retry `i` (0-based) the exponential ceiling is `c = min(cap, base * 2^i)`. Randomness is supplied as
`rand`, a list of integers in `[0, 99]` (percentages) with at least `attempts` entries; retry `i` uses `r = rand[i]`.
All divisions are integer (floor) divisions.

`mode` selects the strategy:

- `"none"`: `delay = c`
- `"full"`: `delay = c * r // 100`
- `"equal"`: `half = c // 2`, `delay = half + (c - half) * r // 100`
- `"decorrelated"`: ignores `c`. With `prev = base` before the first retry,
  `delay = min(cap, base + (3 * prev - base) * r // 100)`, then `prev = delay`.

Return the list of delays.

**Example:** `base = 100`, `cap = 1000`, `attempts = 5`, `mode = "none"`, `rand = [0,0,0,0,0]` → `[100, 200, 400, 800, 1000]`

**Example:** same with `mode = "full"`, `rand = [50, 10, 99, 0, 75]` → `[50, 20, 396, 0, 750]`
net-backoff-jitter.starter:
def backoff_schedule(base: int, cap: int, attempts: int, mode: str, rand: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Timeouts, retries, pools, rate limits and idempotency*.
guide.intuition: Doubling the wait gives an overloaded service room to recover. But if a thousand clients failed at the same instant and all double in lockstep, they come back as synchronised waves. Jitter spreads each wave across the interval; the modes differ only in how much of the interval is randomised.
hints: Compute the capped ceiling first; three of the four modes are one-liners on top of it.
`equal` keeps half the ceiling as a guaranteed minimum and randomises only the other half.
`decorrelated` carries state from one retry to the next: the previous delay.
guide.brute_force: There is nothing slower to write; the brute-force mistake is conceptual: retrying immediately in a tight loop, or with a fixed delay, which is what turns a brief outage into a retry storm.
guide.approach:
1. Loop `i` from 0 to `attempts − 1`, `c = min(cap, base·2^i)`.
2. Apply the formula for the mode with `r = rand[i]`.

**Dry run** `base 100, cap 1000`, full jitter, `rand = [50,10,99,0,75]`: ceilings 100, 200, 400, 800, 1000 → `100·50//100 = 50`, `200·10//100 = 20`, `400·99//100 = 396`, `0`, `750`.
guide.complexity: Time O(attempts), space O(attempts).
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting the cap (after 30 doublings a 100 ms base exceeds a day). Adding jitter on top of the full ceiling in `equal` mode, exceeding the cap. Using the base instead of the previous delay in `decorrelated`. In production also bound the *number* of retries and retry only idempotent operations.
guide.follow_up: Add a retry budget (retries may be at most 10% of requests) and honour a server-supplied `Retry-After`. Compare the total work done by clients under no jitter and full jitter in a simulation.

net-tcp-handshake-validate.title: Validate a TCP Segment Trace
net-tcp-handshake-validate.description:
You are given a capture of one TCP connection on a loss-free, in-order path. Each segment is
`[sender, flags, seq, ack, length]` where `sender` is `"C"` (client) or `"S"` (server), `flags` is one of
`"SYN"`, `"SYN+ACK"`, `"ACK"`, `"FIN+ACK"`, and `length` is the number of payload bytes.

Return `-1` if the whole trace obeys the rules below, otherwise the **index of the first segment that breaks
a rule**. If the trace ends before the three-way handshake is complete, return `len(segments)` (the index
where the missing segment should have been).

**Handshake** (segments 0, 1, 2):

0. from `C`, flags `SYN`, length 0. The client's next sequence number becomes `seq + 1` (a SYN consumes one number).
1. from `S`, flags `SYN+ACK`, length 0, `ack` equal to the client's next sequence number. The server's next becomes `seq + 1`.
2. from `C`, flags `ACK`, length 0, `seq` equal to the client's next, `ack` equal to the server's next.

**After the handshake**, every segment from side X (peer Y) must satisfy all of:

- flags are `ACK` or `FIN+ACK`;
- `seq` equals X's next sequence number;
- `ack` is at most Y's next sequence number (you cannot acknowledge bytes never sent) and at least the last `ack` value X sent (acknowledgements never move backwards). The last `ack` sent by C starts at the value in segment 2; by S, at the value in segment 1;
- if X has already sent a FIN, the segment must be a plain `ACK` with length 0.

Then X's next sequence number grows by `length`, plus 1 if the segment carries FIN.

**Example:** `[["C","SYN",100,0,0], ["S","SYN+ACK",300,101,0], ["C","ACK",101,301,0], ["C","ACK",101,301,5], ["S","ACK",301,106,0]]` → `-1`

**Example:** the same trace with the server's last ack changed to `107` → `4`

guide.prereqs: The lesson *UDP and the TCP connection lifecycle*: sequence and acknowledgement numbers, SYN and FIN each consuming one sequence number.
guide.intuition: Keep one counter per side: the next sequence number that side will use. A segment is legal when it starts exactly at its sender's counter and acknowledges no more than the peer's counter. SYN and FIN are 'phantom bytes' that advance the counter by one.
hints: Handle the first three segments as three explicit special cases; they have fixed senders and flags.
After the handshake you need four pieces of state: `next[C]`, `next[S]`, the last ack each side sent, and whether each side has sent FIN.
The acknowledgement must lie in the closed range `[last ack this side sent, peer's next]`.
guide.brute_force: Re-derive each side's byte count from scratch for every segment by summing the lengths of all earlier segments: O(n²). Carrying running counters makes it one pass.
guide.approach:
1. Check segments 0–2 against the handshake rules, returning the index of the first failure or `len(segments)` if the trace is too short.
2. Initialise the running state and scan the rest, applying the four established-state checks in order.
3. Advance the sender's counter by `length` (+1 for FIN) and remember its ack.

**Dry run** (example 1): after the handshake `next = {C:101, S:301}`. Segment 3: C sends 5 bytes at seq 101 ✓, ack 301 ≤ 301 ✓ → `next[C] = 106`. Segment 4: S at seq 301 ✓, ack 106 ≤ 106 ✓. Result `-1`. With ack 107 the server would be acknowledging a byte the client never sent → index 4.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls: Forgetting that SYN and FIN consume a sequence number (acks will look off by one). Checking only an upper bound on the ack. Allowing data after a FIN: a side that has sent FIN may still *receive* and acknowledge data (half-close) but may not send more.
guide.follow_up: Extend the checker to tolerate retransmissions and out-of-order arrival, or to report the final state of each endpoint (ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT, TIME_WAIT, CLOSED).

net-cwnd-evolution.title: Congestion Window Evolution
net-cwnd-evolution.description:
Trace a simplified TCP Reno congestion window, measured in whole segments (MSS), one step per round trip.

The window starts at `cwnd = 1` with the given initial `ssthresh`. `events[i]` says what happened to the
window of data sent in round `i`:

- `"ok"`: everything was acknowledged.
  - If `cwnd < ssthresh` (slow start): `cwnd = min(2 * cwnd, ssthresh)`.
  - Otherwise (congestion avoidance): `cwnd = cwnd + 1`.
- `"3dup"`: loss detected by three duplicate ACKs (fast retransmit / fast recovery):
  `ssthresh = max(cwnd // 2, 2)`, then `cwnd = ssthresh`.
- `"timeout"`: loss detected by the retransmission timer:
  `ssthresh = max(cwnd // 2, 2)`, then `cwnd = 1`.

Return the list of `cwnd` values: the value at the start of every round followed by the final value
(so the result has `len(events) + 1` entries).

**Example:** `ssthresh = 8`, `events = ["ok","ok","ok","ok","3dup","ok"]` → `[1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 4, 5]`
net-cwnd-evolution.starter:
def cwnd_trace(ssthresh: int, events: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Flow control and congestion control*: slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and recovery.
guide.intuition: It is a tiny state machine with two variables. `ssthresh` remembers where trouble was last met; below it the window doubles, above it the window creeps up by one. A mild loss signal halves the window, a severe one collapses it to one.
hints: Record the window *before* applying each event, then append the final value once at the end (or start the list with 1 and append after each event).
Slow start must not overshoot: cap the doubling at `ssthresh`.
Both loss events set `ssthresh` from the *current* `cwnd` before changing `cwnd`.
guide.brute_force: There is no asymptotically slower approach worth writing: the simulation is inherently one pass. A common first attempt handles only the `ok` case and bolts the loss cases on afterwards.
guide.approach:
1. `cwnd = 1`, output `[1]`.
2. For each event update `(cwnd, ssthresh)` by the rule for that event, then append `cwnd`.

**Dry run** `ssthresh = 8`, events `ok ok ok ok 3dup ok`:

| round | cwnd before | event | ssthresh after | cwnd after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | ok (slow start) | 8 | 2 |
| 1 | 2 | ok | 8 | 4 |
| 2 | 4 | ok | 8 | 8 |
| 3 | 8 | ok (avoidance) | 8 | 9 |
| 4 | 9 | 3dup | 4 | 4 |
| 5 | 4 | ok (avoidance, 4 ≥ 4) | 4 | 5 |
guide.complexity: Time O(n) for n events; space O(n) for the output.
guide.pitfalls: Doubling past `ssthresh` (e.g. 4 → 8 when ssthresh is 6). Treating three duplicate ACKs like a timeout (that is TCP Tahoe). Computing the new `cwnd` before the new `ssthresh`. Using `<=` in the slow-start test: at `cwnd == ssthresh` the sender is already in congestion avoidance.
guide.follow_up: Model CUBIC's cubic growth function, or count total segments delivered to compare the throughput of Tahoe and Reno on the same loss pattern.

net-sliding-window-sender.title: Sliding-Window Sender with Cumulative ACKs
net-sliding-window-sender.description:
A sender must deliver packets numbered `0 .. total - 1` using a window of `window` packets and
Go-Back-N recovery. It keeps two counters: `base` (the oldest unacknowledged packet) and `next`
(the next never-sent packet). At any time it may have sent only packets `p` with `p < base + window`.

Whenever it is allowed to, the sender immediately transmits new packets in increasing order until the window
is full or nothing is left.

`events` is a list of integers processed in order:

- a value `a >= 0` is a **cumulative ACK**: the receiver has everything below `a`. If `base < a <= next`,
  set `base = a`; otherwise ignore it (stale or impossible).
- `-1` is a **timeout**: retransmit every outstanding packet `base .. next - 1` in order.

Return a list of lists: first the packets transmitted at start-up, then, for each event, the packets
transmitted in reaction to it (retransmissions first, then any new packets the window now allows).

**Example:** `total = 6`, `window = 3`, `events = [1, 3, -1, 6]` → `[[0,1,2], [3], [4,5], [3,4,5], []]`
net-sliding-window-sender.starter:
def sender_trace(total: int, window: int, events: list) -> list:
    pass

guide.prereqs: The lesson *Flow control and congestion control* (sliding windows); cumulative acknowledgements.
guide.intuition: The window is the half-open range `[base, base + window)`. ACKs slide its left edge to the right, which opens room on the right for new packets. A timeout does not move the window; it just replays what is inside it.
hints: Write one helper that sends new packets while `next < base + window` and `next < total`; call it after every event.
A cumulative ACK `a` can acknowledge several packets at once: set `base = a`, not `base += 1`.
Ignore ACKs that do not advance `base` or that claim packets you never sent.
guide.brute_force: Track a boolean 'acked' flag per packet and rescan from 0 on every event to find the window: O(total) per event. Two integer counters carry the same information.
guide.approach:
1. `base = next = 0`; transmit the first window.
2. ACK `a`: if `base < a <= next` then `base = a`; then top the window up.
3. Timeout: output `base .. next-1`, then top up (normally nothing new fits).

**Dry run** `total=6, window=3, events=[1,3,-1,6]`:

| event | base | next | transmitted |
|---|---|---|---|
| start | 0 | 3 | 0 1 2 |
| ack 1 | 1 | 4 | 3 |
| ack 3 | 3 | 6 | 4 5 |
| timeout | 3 | 6 | 3 4 5 |
| ack 6 | 6 | 6 | (nothing) |
guide.complexity: Time O(total + number of retransmitted packets + events); space O(output).
guide.pitfalls: Letting a stale ACK move `base` backwards (duplicates of old ACKs are normal). Accepting an ACK beyond `next`. Sending past `total`. Forgetting that a timeout with an empty window produces an empty list.
guide.follow_up: Replace Go-Back-N with selective repeat (per-packet timers and a receiver buffer), or add a receiver-advertised window that changes with each ACK.

net-gbn-vs-sr.title: Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat Transmission Counts
net-gbn-vs-sr.description:
Compare how many data transmissions two ARQ schemes need to deliver packets `0 .. n - 1` with window `window`.

Losses are described per attempt: `lost` contains pairs `[packet, attempt]` meaning the `attempt`-th
transmission (1-based) of that packet is lost. Acknowledgements are never lost, and every packet eventually
gets through.

Both protocols work in rounds, starting with `base = 0`:

**Go-Back-N.** While `base < n`: transmit packets `base .. min(base + window, n) - 1` in order (each counts as
one more attempt of that packet). The receiver accepts only in-order packets, so let `f` be the first packet
of this round whose transmission was lost. If there is one, set `base = f` (everything after it in the round
was wasted); otherwise `base` moves to the end of the round.

**Selective Repeat.** While `base < n`: transmit every packet in `base .. min(base + window, n) - 1` that has
**not yet been received** (one more attempt each); those not lost become received. Then advance `base` past
all consecutively received packets.

Return `[gbn_transmissions, sr_transmissions]`.

**Example:** `n = 5`, `window = 3`, `lost = [[1, 1]]` → `[7, 6]`

(GBN sends 0 1 2, loses 1, goes back and sends 1 2 3, then 4. SR sends 0 1 2, then 1 3 4.)
